extracted.intended_audience: early-career (and other) researchers asked to review journal manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for how to conduct fair, rigorous, and ethical peer review of scientific journal manuscripts, including what to check in introductions, methods, results, and broader ethical/procedural responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself honestly whether this paper falls within the scope of your expertise; if it falls too far outside your discipline and knowledge, it’s better to leave the review to someone else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you decline, do so promptly to avoid delaying the process and recommend several alternate referees to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an effort to return a review within the specified deadline because people’s research careers may depend on how quickly their papers are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider your schedule and the time required (newer reviewers may need many additional hours); if you cannot commit, decline or request an extension before accepting. Example: some reviews may take 8–10 hours plus additional time for revised versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take it seriously / Rigor of review
rubrics_metrics.description: The review must be rigorous; don’t sign off on a paper or do a slapdash job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read critically; the review should ideally help authors improve their manuscript and contribute to the overall quality of the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bias and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not review a manuscript if you have a strong (positive or negative) feeling about any of the authors, or if you have any possible conflict of interest (e.g., past collaboration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, declare your possible conflict before agreeing. Be deliberate about reviewing the manuscript in front of you, not the authors or their location; be aware of implicit biases (e.g., gender bias) reported in studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use review for personal/professional advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not review with any intention of reaping personal or professional benefit from it (for example, to slow a competing lab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such behavior is extremely unethical and can be grounds for a formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be intimidated by authors’ stature
rubrics_metrics.description: Academia’s implicit hierarchy should not apply when reviewing—big names are not automatically right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work on its merits regardless of author reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not talk about the manuscript, its results, or its methods with outsiders or use information from the manuscript prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not communicate with the authors about their manuscript; all thoughts and comments should only go to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough reading and iterative review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the entirety of the submission (including Supplementary Online Information) several times and take notes constantly before drafting your response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft your review only after multiple readings; if needed ask the editor privately for additional expert reviewers for specific portions you cannot assess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive, professional tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being unnecessarily harsh or abusive; criticism should be constructive in tone—peer review is not the place to demonstrate wit or disrespect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference specific parts of the manuscript (for example by line number) to anchor criticisms and suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Introduction / Background for relevance and literature coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the questions addressed advance the field in a meaningful way and whether appropriate references are cited and emphasized correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If references are missing or inappropriately emphasized, identify specific omissions and suggest citations; perform your own literature search as if you were writing the paper; it’s fine to suggest authors cite your work when appropriate but do not demand self-citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Approach / Methods for sufficiency and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should provide enough detail in methods and materials such that you can fully understand their experiments and others can replicate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If methods are unclear, ask for clarification or additional detail; consult outside sources or colleagues (while respecting confidentiality) to assess methods; if you’re not confident, tell the editor and request an additional expert to review that portion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious and justified when requesting additional experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: You may request different or additional experiments, but such requests must be justified for verifying reported results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind time, effort, and cost to authors; do not request experiments to unfairly delay publication or advantage your own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Results / Interpretation and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the data support the authors’ interpretations and whether results are presented clearly and appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for more results or better ways of presenting them when needed; recommend statistical or other specialist review if interpretation appears to require it; suggest moving material between Supplementary Online Information and main text where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final checks: writing quality, statements, data and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that writing is clear and reasonably free of grammatical errors, and review associated statements (Funders Statement, Ethics Statement, Conflict of Interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request additional editing if writing is unclear; confirm authors specify data availability (mechanism to make raw data available) and protection of human subjects (e.g., in genomics); include these considerations in your write-up to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity versus open review considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether to sign your review: open review may increase effort, credit, and accountability, while anonymity may make some reviewers—especially early-career—feel more comfortable critiquing colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand journal policies (PeerJ encourages but does not require open review) and make a personal decision; signing can provide public credit and allow others to learn from your reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in post-publication peer review and community critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that publication is the beginning of evaluation; post-publication comments, replication, and community assessment are important components of quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use platforms such as journal comment systems, PubPeer, or PubMed Commons to comment on published work when appropriate; post-publication reviewing enables anyone to act as a reviewer after publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous improvement through practice and study
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve reviewing skills by practicing (doing reviews), participating in journal clubs, studying other reviewers’ comments, and experiencing the process as an author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading review histories and comments on articles can teach approaches to reviewing; being an author helps you learn how to give and receive reviews effectively; view reviewing as a civic contribution to the scientific community.
